faq.a: No; combine CVP with clinical exam, lactate, urine output, and ultrasound for a balanced picture.
faq.q: Can CVP be used alone to decide fluid therapy?

faq.a: Vasodilation and increased capillary leak can keep right‑atrial pressure near normal while tissue perfusion is poor.
faq.q: Why is CVP often normal in septic shock despite hypovolemia?

faq.a: Not always; in early resuscitation of trauma a modest rise may reflect adequate preload, but persistent elevation signals overload.
faq.q: Is a high CVP always bad?

exam: A patient with penetrating abdominal trauma is hypotensive, tachycardic, and has flat neck veins. What is the next step and why? — Estimate CVP clinically; low CVP suggests hemorrhagic shock, so give rapid crystalloid and arrange blood transfusion.

During management of severe malaria, a patient develops jugular venous distension and peripheral edema. How does this change your fluid plan? — High CVP indicates fluid overload; stop aggressive fluids, start diuretics, and monitor renal function.

You obtain a CVP of 12 cm H₂O in a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism. What does this tell you? — Elevated CVP suggests right‑ventricular strain; urgent anticoagulation and consider thrombolysis.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with shock; CVP is 4 cm H₂O. What are the likely causes and immediate management? — Low CVP points to hypovolemia from vaso‑occlusive crisis or sepsis; give isotonic fluids and treat underlying infection.
Why might a patient on non‑invasive ventilation have a falsely high CVP reading? — Positive airway pressure increases intrathoracic pressure, raising right‑atrial pressure without true volume excess.

Explain how you would differentiate cardiac tamponade from severe right‑heart failure using CVP and bedside findings. — Both raise CVP, but tamponade shows pulsus paradoxus and clear lungs; right‑heart failure shows peripheral edema and hepatomegaly.
In a resource‑limited setting without a central line, how can you reliably assess volume status? — Use jugular venous height, IVC ultrasound, capillary refill, and urine output together.

What are the risks of giving large fluid boluses to a patient with high CVP and how can you monitor for them? — Risk of pulmonary edema and worsening heart failure; monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, lung auscultation, and repeat CVP.
ai.title: Central Venous Pressure
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Central venous pressure (CVP) estimates right‑atrial pressure and guides fluid management in shock and heart failure. It is measured at the bedside with a catheter or estimated clinically by jugular venous assessment.

b: Invasive CVP: zero at the mid‑axillary line, transducer at the level of the right atrium.
Clinical estimate: vertical distance (cm H₂O) from the right atrium to the top of the jugular pulsation.
sections.p: CVP is the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting preload and intravascular volume. It can be measured invasively with a central line or estimated by the height of the internal jugular venous pulsation.

b: Low CVP < 5 cm H₂O – hypovolemia or distributive shock.
Normal CVP 5–10 cm H₂O – euvolemia.
High CVP > 10 cm H₂O – fluid overload, right‑heart failure, tamponade.
sections.p: CVP values guide the degree of volume depletion or overload.

b: Low CVP: severe dehydration, hemorrhage, septic shock, adrenal insufficiency.
High CVP: right‑ventricular infarction, pulmonary embolism, constrictive pericarditis, severe anemia, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease with fluid overload.
sections.p: Identify why CVP is abnormal before treating.

b: Low CVP: tachycardia, hypotension, cold clammy skin, flat neck veins.
High CVP: jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, pulsus paradoxus in tamponade.
sections.p: Patients with abnormal CVP show signs that match the underlying cause.

t.b: Is the patient volume depleted or overloaded? – A visible pulsation > 3 cm above the sternal angle suggests high CVP; absent pulsation suggests low CVP.
What is the exact pressure? – Gives numeric value to guide fluid therapy; if unavailable, rely on clinical estimate.
Is right‑heart function impaired? – Dilated IVC with < 50 % collapse on inspiration supports high CVP; collapsible IVC supports low CVP.
Are there signs of fluid overload or tamponade? – Enlarged cardiac silhouette or pleural effusion may explain high CVP.
Is there bleeding or metabolic shock? – Low Hb with high lactate points to hemorrhagic hypovolemia.

b: Persistent low CVP → irreversible organ hypoperfusion, acute kidney injury.
Persistent high CVP → hepatic congestion, bowel edema, worsening heart failure, cardiac arrest.
sections.p: Uncorrected extremes of CVP can be fatal.

b: Low CVP: rapid isotonic crystalloid bolus (e.g., normal saline) until CVP rises to 8–10 cm H₂O; consider blood products if hemorrhage.
High CVP: diuretics (loop diuretics) to reduce preload; treat right‑heart failure with ACE‑inhibitors or beta‑blockers when appropriate; consider ultrafiltration if diuretics fail.
Avoid excessive fluids in patients with high CVP because they worsen pulmonary edema.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then adjust fluids while monitoring CVP.

b: Document CVP trend on the chart; aim for target range based on diagnosis.
Educate patients on fluid restriction in chronic heart failure.
In trauma, use early point‑of‑care ultrasound to guide resuscitation.
sections.p: Re‑measure CVP after each intervention and adjust therapy.

b: Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) – reflects left‑atrial pressure, not right‑atrial.
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) – systemic arterial pressure, unrelated to preload.
sections.p: Distinguish CVP from other pressure measurements.

b: Positive pressure ventilation raises CVP without true volume overload.
Obesity or neck masses can make jugular assessment inaccurate.
Catheter transducer zeroing error can give falsely high or low numbers.
sections.p: Be aware of factors that alter CVP interpretation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of jugular pulsation with hypotension – possible massive hemorrhage.
Rapidly rising CVP with muffled heart sounds – cardiac tamponade.
Severe dyspnea and CVP > 15 cm H₂O – acute decompensated right‑heart failure.
